title: How the Reading Incentive Program Works in Public Schools
seoTitle: How Brazil's public schools run reading incentive program
subtitle: Explore the pedagogical backstage, the complex distribution logistics, and the social impact of the public policy that supplies school libraries across Brazil.
excerpt: Learn how the selection, purchase, and distribution of literary books for millions of students in Brazil's public education network operate.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The distribution of literary and textbook volumes to Brazilian public schools is one of the largest and most complex logistics and pedagogy operations in the contemporary world. Every year, millions of students from urban, rural, Indigenous and riverside areas receive in their classrooms volumes that serve as the foundation for formal learning and for an introduction to the world of fiction, poetry and essays. Understanding how this gear works reveals how the State acts to guarantee democratic access to written culture in a country marked by deep socioeconomic inequalities.

The book's journey from publisher to the student's backpack

The public policy for acquiring and distributing books to the public education network operates through a structured partnership between the Ministry of Education and the National Fund for Education Development. The core goal is to ensure that all students enrolled in basic education—including early childhood, primary and secondary education—have free access to high‑quality teaching materials and literary collections. This joint action aims to mitigate book scarcity in low‑income households, promoting educational equity nationwide.

The program’s workflow follows a multi‑year cycle planned almost two years in advance for each schooling stage. It begins with the publication of public call notices, in which the Ministry of Education sets the pedagogical, technical and physical specifications that books must meet. Private‑sector publishers and independent authors submit their works, which undergo a rigorous technical screening before being made available for schools to choose from. This mechanism ensures that the country’s publishing output is widely evaluated, selecting only works that demonstrate textual and graphic excellence.

A key feature of the Brazilian model is the decentralisation of the final choice. While the federal government conducts the technical assessment and finances bulk purchases, the decision on which books will be adopted in each classroom rests exclusively with teachers and managers of each school unit. This format respects schools’ pedagogical autonomy and allows educators to select titles that best fit the cultural, social and economic reality of their community, making teaching more meaningful and contextualised.

The evolution of book‑distribution policies in Brazil

The Brazilian State’s concern with school‑book distribution dates back to the first half of the 20th century, when the country sought to modernise public institutions and expand basic‑education access. In the late 1930s, the first federal body specifically dedicated to formulating a national textbook policy was created. Its initial focus was standardising curricular content and combating the high illiteracy rates that limited the nation’s social development.

In the following decades, around the mid‑20th century, the state model underwent deep operational transformations. The federal government stopped producing and printing books directly, becoming instead a purchaser and distributor of works produced by the private publishing market. This shift stimulated growth of Brazil’s graphic and publishing industry, which professionalised to meet the technical requirements and large volumes demanded by the public sector, consolidating a robust and competitive book market.

At the turn of the millennium, the public reading‑incentive policy made a qualitative leap by systematically incorporating the distribution of specific literary collections for school libraries and classrooms. Until then, distribution mainly focused on textbooks for traditional subjects. The realisation that forming a proficient reader requires direct contact with fiction, poetry, theatre and children‑and‑youth literature led to programmes dedicated exclusively to building diverse literary collections, expanding the cultural repertoire of students of all ages.

Behind the scenes of literary‑work evaluation and selection

The selection process for literary works that will become part of school libraries is characterised by rigorous technical and pedagogical scrutiny. After publishers submit their titles, the Ministry of Education convenes evaluation commissions composed of teachers and researchers from public universities across all regions. These specialists conduct an individual, blind technical analysis of each book, ensuring impartiality and preventing commercial or political interference.

Pedagogical evaluation criteria are comprehensive and detailed in the call notices. Reviewers assess the aesthetic quality of the text, the suitability of language for the indicated age group, the coherence between written text and illustrations, and the work’s potential to spark spontaneous reading interest. There is also a strict requirement that the works promote respect for cultural diversity, gender equality, ethnic‑racial minority rights and environmental preservation; books that convey prejudice, stereotypes or discrimination are promptly disqualified.

The digital guide creation and teacher autonomy

Works approved by the expert commissions are catalogued in a detailed digital guide prepared by the Ministry of Education. This guide contains critical reviews, pedagogical analyses and classroom‑use suggestions for each selected book. The material serves as a resource for state and municipal teachers to learn about available options and make choices based on solid technical criteria.

The selection period is an intense pedagogical activity within public schools. Teachers gather in faculty councils to study the guide, discuss their students’ needs and record their choices in an online system managed by the National Fund for Education Development. To guarantee continuous supply even if a particular publisher’s stock runs out, each school must indicate a first and a second collection option for every education segment.

The logistical gear that supplies classrooms nationwide

After schools across the country finalise their choices, the National Fund for Education Development begins price negotiations and contracts with publishers for book production. Because of the massive purchase volume, the federal government can negotiate unit prices far below retail market rates, optimising public‑fund use and ensuring the programme’s economic efficiency.

The physical distribution of books is a gigantic logistical operation that requires meticulous planning of road, rail, air and river routes. Brazil’s postal service, Correios, plays a central role, using its extensive network to deliver packages directly to thousands of school units spread from major metropolises to the most isolated communities.

  • Road transport: Trucks cross the country, moving loads from printing houses concentrated in the South and Southeast to regional distribution centres.
  • River transport: In the Amazon region, boats and ferries carry boxes of books along rivers, reaching riverside and Indigenous schools without road access.
  • Delivery control: The tracking system allows school managers and education secretariats to monitor cargo movement in real time, ensuring process transparency.
  • Reallocation of stock: If a school’s enrolment numbers change after the order closes, local secretariats physically reallocate surplus copies to avoid material waste.

Accessibility and inclusion in school reading formats

Democratising reading access presumes that every student, without exception, can use the books provided by the public power. For this reason, the reading‑incentive policy incorporates specific guidelines for producing accessible materials for students with visual, auditory or intellectual disabilities. This inclusion effort aims to make the school library a welcoming space for the full diversity of learners.

Purchase calls require publishers to provide adapted versions of approved works. For blind or low‑vision students, books are produced in Braille and enlarged‑character formats, alongside audiobooks narrated professionally and equipped with audio description of illustrations. The National Fund for Education Development also acquires and distributes digital accessible versions that can be read by screen‑reader software on computers and tablets supplied to multifunctional resource rooms.

Inclusion also extends to deaf students through the distribution of teaching and literary materials that include translation and interpretation in Brazilian Sign Language (Libras). The presence of these resources in public schools not only guarantees the learning rights of students with disabilities but also raises awareness among all pupils about the importance of accessibility and living with human diversity, enriching the whole school environment.

Myths about the choice and content of school books

The sheer scale of the national book‑distribution programme sometimes generates misinformation and doubts among civil society. One persistent myth is that the federal government imposes a single, centrally‑controlled curriculum and textbook authoritatively across the entire nation. As explained earlier, the process is decentralised: the federal government acts as technical evaluator and bulk purchaser, but the final adoption decision rests solely with each school’s teaching staff, respecting regional specificities and local pedagogical autonomy.

Another common misconception concerns the destination and ownership of distributed books. Many believe that literary books sent to schools are for classroom‑only use and that students cannot take them home. In reality, reading‑incentive guidelines promote systematic home‑loaning of literary works, allowing books to circulate among families and help create a reading‑friendly environment at home. For consumable textbooks aimed at early childhood and the first years of primary school, the works become the student’s permanent property at the end of the school year.

There is also the false perception that literary‑work selection is influenced by the ruling party’s political preferences. The evaluation process is shielded by strictly technical and scientific criteria defined in transparent public calls, overseen by independent academic commissions linked to public universities. Evaluators’ decisions are based on public technical reports that any citizen can consult, ensuring the integrity and continuity of the State policy regardless of political changes.

The impact of school libraries on citizen formation

An active, well‑stocked school library has a profound impact on the cognitive, social and cultural development of public‑school students. Data from Brazil’s National Institute for Educational Studies and Research (INEP) show that schools with structured libraries and regular reading‑mediation activities achieve higher scores on national proficiency exams in Portuguese and mathematics, evidencing a direct correlation between book access and academic success.

Beyond academic indicators, literary reading serves as an essential tool for developing empathy, imagination and critical thinking. By encountering realities different from their own through literature, young readers broaden their geographic and social horizons, improve their ability to express ideas clearly and gain greater intellectual autonomy to interpret the world around them.

School libraries also play a significant social role by acting as cultural hubs within vulnerable communities. In many parts of Brazil, the public‑school library is the only free cultural space available to residents. When the school opens its doors for community events such as poetry evenings, reading clubs and storytelling sessions, it strengthens communal bonds and brings families closer to their children’s learning environment, creating a virtuous circle of valuing education and culture.

Frequently asked questions about public literary‑book access

To facilitate understanding of the programme’s practical operation, we gathered answers to the most common questions from parents, students and school managers about collection distribution.

How does a public school request new books for its collection?

Public schools participate in the selection process periodically, according to the schedule set by the Ministry of Education for each education level. School managers must log into the National Fund for Education Development’s online system during the selection window and record the options decided by the faculty council. Schools that do not submit choices receive a standard book load technically defined by the federal body to ensure no student lacks material.

What happens if a school does not receive books at the start of the academic year?

If delivery delays or inconsistencies occur, the school principal must log the incident in the programme’s monitoring system. The National Fund for Education Development and local education secretariats analyse the case to identify logistical failures or arrange the reallocation of surplus copies from other schools in the same region, guaranteeing rapid resupply of the affected unit.

Do literary books need to be returned to the school at the end of the year?

Yes. Literary books that belong to the school library or classroom reading corners are considered public heritage and must be returned to the school at the end of each academic year. This return is essential so the works can be used by new student cohorts in subsequent years, promoting sustainability and preservation of public assets.

How can society monitor the resources applied to the programme?

Any citizen can follow the use of public funds for book purchases through the federal government’s transparency portals and the National Fund for Education Development’s website. These online channels provide detailed data on contracts with publishers, unit prices paid for each work, the quantity of books allocated to each municipality and delivery reports from transport companies and Correios.

Consolidating a reading culture in education networks

The success of a reading‑incentive policy in public schools is not limited to physically delivering books to students’ desks. Supplying literary collections is only the first step of a complex process that requires continuous reading‑mediation actions and the valorisation of the book as a cultural object. For books to come alive and transform students’ realities, the active role of teachers and librarians as mediators between text and reader is indispensable.

Ongoing teacher training for reading mediation is a strategic guideline championed by UNESCO as a pathway to building a reading society. Well‑trained teachers know how to select the most suitable works for each stage of their pupils’ development, propose shared‑reading activities that stimulate critical debate, and create a welcoming environment where reading is seen as a source of pleasure and discovery rather than a mere school obligation.

Thus, by ensuring the regular delivery of high‑quality aesthetic and pedagogical literary collections to millions of children and youth across the country, Brazil establishes a State policy that transcends governments and generations. Investing in the formation of new readers in public schools represents a fundamental step toward reducing sociocultural inequalities, guaranteeing every citizen the inalienable right to knowledge, literature and imagination.
